01.r: The whole body of believers, taken as one company.

02.r: Moves to a summary of the community's life.

03.n: Abbott-Smith: 'a great number, a multitude', used of things and of persons. The noun is in the genitive: literally 'of the multitude ... the heart and soul was one'.

04.r: The article turns 'having believed' into a description of people.

05.r: Those who had come to faith.
05.n: Abbott-Smith: 'to have faith (in), to believe'. An aorist participle, looking at the coming to faith as an event; the earlier summary of the community uses a present participle, 'those believing'.

06.r: With the genitive before it, says what the multitude had: one heart and soul.
06.n: Greek says 'of the multitude ... was one heart and soul', a way of saying they had one heart and soul, as the DRC renders it.

08.r: The centre of thought, will and feeling, here shared as if by one person.
08.n: Abbott-Smith gives the bodily organ first, then the heart 'in a psychological sense, the seat of man's collective energies, the focus of personal life'.

11.r: The inner self; with 'heart', it describes one shared mind and will.
11.n: This study renders ψυχή 'soul' or 'life' by context. Here, joined with 'heart', it is the inner self, not physical life. Abbott-Smith notes it very frequently stands for Hebrew נֶפֶשׁ in the Septuagint.

12.r: Heart and soul were one, as if the whole company were one person.
12.n: A single 'one' covers both nouns; the KJV, Geneva and DRC repeat it.

13.r: Adds the practical result of their unity.

14.r: Stresses that there was no exception at all.
14.n: Abbott-Smith gives this word as a conjunction, 'and not, also not, neither, nor', and as an adverb. Before 'one' it has the adverb's force, 'not even one'.

16.r: Any item at all of what he had.

17.r: The article with the participle that follows: the things that belonged to him.

18.r: What each believer had, his possessions.
18.n: A participle of ὑπάρχω, 'to be at hand'; with the article it means one's possessions. Abbott-Smith notes that in the Septuagint τὰ ὑπάρχοντα stands for Hebrew words such as מִקְנֶה and רְכוּשׁ, livestock and goods.

19.r: The things belonging to the man in question.
19.n: A dative of the owner: 'the things being to him', that is, his possessions.

20.r: No one was making a claim of private ownership.
20.n: An imperfect: describes a settled attitude over time, not one statement.

21.r: Private property, set against what was common.
21.n: Abbott-Smith: 'one's own', of what is private and personal, and he notes that in classical Greek it is the opposite of κοινός, 'common'. This verse sets the two words against each other.

22.r: The infinitive of the reported claim: 'to be his own'.

23.r: Sets the true state of things against the denied claim.
23.n: Abbott-Smith calls it an adversative particle stronger than δέ.

24.n: With the dative 'to them', literally 'all things were common to them', which the KJV turns into 'they had all things common'.

25.r: The believers as a body, to whom all things belonged in common.

26.n: Abbott-Smith calls this a strengthened form of πᾶς, 'all'.

27.r: What belonged to each was treated as belonging to all.
27.n: Abbott-Smith files this verse, with Acts 2:44, under 'common (general; = Lat. communis)'. His second sense, ordinary and so unhallowed or unclean, does not apply here.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus has the article with both nouns, 'the heart and the soul', which does not show in the KJV. Where our text has αὐτῷ, 'to him' (the things belonging to him), the data behind this study records the Textus Receptus as reading αὐτῶν, 'of them'; the KJV's 'any of them' fits that reading, though 'of them' is natural English here either way and the ASV has it too.
